idiom_name: final class NullCustomer implements Customer + static final INSTANCE
implementation_notes: For your own interface the realization is still Woolf's: a final class NullCustomer implements Customer whose methods return neutral values, exposed as a static final Customer INSTANCE (or an enum singleton) so nothing allocates per call. java.util.Optional is the complement, not the same thing: use Optional<Customer> when the caller must act on absence, and the null implementation when it must not. Modern Java adds no new mechanism for this, and implementing the interface is preferable to extending the real class, because a subclass silently inherits methods added later.
pitfalls: Optional is not a null object: Optional.empty() still forces the caller to unwrap, and an Optional field is discouraged (it is not Serializable), so keep the null instance in fields and use Optional only at return boundaries.
Letting the null class extend the real class couples it to the superclass's state and silently inherits new methods; implement the interface and mark the null class final.
The shared INSTANCE is a static, so mutable state in the null object is shared with every caller - keep it stateless, otherwise 'neutral' behaviour stops being neutral.

variants.name: JDK-provided shared null objects (empty collections, null streams)
variants.implementation_notes: For collection, iterator and stream interfaces the JDK already ships the null object: Collections.emptyList(), emptySet(), emptyMap() and emptyIterator() return shared immutable instances whose operations are neutral (mutation throws UnsupportedOperationException by contract), and Java 11 added InputStream.nullInputStream() ('returns a new InputStream that reads no bytes') and OutputStream.nullOutputStream() ('discards all bytes'). Returning these instead of null for 'no results' removes the null check from every loop without writing a class; the hand-written variant is then needed only for domain interfaces. List.of()/Map.of() (Java 9) are the immutable-collection factory equivalents.
variants.code_sketch:
List<Order> orders = repository.findByCustomer(id);   // never returns null
for (Order o : orders) { charge(o); }                 // zero iterations if none

Iterator<Order> it = Collections.emptyIterator();     // shared, immutable
InputStream empty = InputStream.nullInputStream();    // Java 11: reads no bytes
pitfalls: The JDK empties are immutable: Collections.emptyList().add(x) throws UnsupportedOperationException - the right contract for a null object, but it breaks callers that treat an empty result as a list they may fill.
Identity comparison with Collections.emptyList() is an implementation detail, not a way to detect the null case; other empty lists are just as empty.
Optional<List<X>> overlaps with these null objects and forces a check for an empty container as well as an empty list; pick one convention per API and keep it.
